props.title: Man on the Flying Trapeze
props.initialSlug: Family man's white lies spiral into comic chaos

sections.content: W.C. Fields delivers one of his finest performances in **Man on the Flying Trapeze (1935)** (1935), showcasing his masterful blend of verbal wit and physical comedy. The film exemplifies Fields' signature portrayal of the put-upon everyman, building on the foundation he established in It's a Gift (1934) and **The Old Fashioned Way** (1934). As memory expert Ambrose Wolfinger, Fields crafts a character struggling against domineering family members, workplace absurdity, and the general chaos of Depression-era America.

sections.content: The film's influence on subsequent comedy cannot be overstated. Its exploration of workplace deception and family dynamics laid groundwork for later classics like **The Apartment** (1960) and **Nine to Five** (1980). Fields' expert timing and ability to build comedic sequences influenced physical comedians from Jacques Tati to Rowan Atkinson. The memorable burglary scene, where Wolfinger confronts incompetent thieves, became a template for similar sequences in films like **Home Alone** (1990). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Physical Comedy

Fields' work in **Man on the Flying Trapeze** (1935) represents a crucial bridge between silent-era slapstick and modern comedy. His combination of verbal wit and physical business influenced directors like Preston Sturges, whose **Sullivan's Travels** (1941) paid homage to this style. The film's office sequences, particularly Wolfinger's attempts to leave work for a wrestling match, established patterns still seen in workplace comedies like **Office Space** (1999).
